title: Pigeonhole Bin Function for Fractional Parts
content: The binning infrastructure for Dirichlet's theorem. `binFn α N hN : Fin(N+1) → Fin(N)` maps each index i to the bin ⌊N · fract(iα)⌋ ∈ {0,...,N-1}. Two supporting lemmas establish the bin function is well-typed: `floor_mul_fract_nonneg` proves ⌊N · fract(x)⌋ ≥ 0 (from non-negativity of N and fract), and `floor_mul_fract_lt` proves ⌊N · fract(x)⌋ < N (from fract(x) < 1 and positivity of N). The `same_bin_fract_close` lemma then shows that two values landing in the same bin have fractional parts within 1/N of each other, using the floor sandwich: k ≤ N·fract(x) < k+1 for both values implies their difference is less than 1/N after dividing by N.
mathContext: The bin function $\text{bin}(i) = \lfloor N \cdot \{i\alpha\} \rfloor$ partitions $[0,1)$ into $N$ equal intervals $[k/N, (k+1)/N)$ for $k = 0, \ldots, N-1$. If $\text{bin}(i) = \text{bin}(j) = k$, then both $\{i\alpha\}$ and $\{j\alpha\}$ lie in $[k/N, (k+1)/N)$, so $|\{i\alpha\} - \{j\alpha\}| < 1/N$.

title: Dirichlet's Approximation Theorem (1842)
content: The main theorem: for any real α and N ≥ 1, there exist integers p, q with 1 ≤ q ≤ N and |qα - p| < 1/N. The proof invokes `Fintype.exists_ne_map_eq_of_card_lt` (pigeonhole) on `binFn`: since |Fin(N+1)| > |Fin(N)|, two distinct indices i ≠ j must collide. Their fractional parts differ by < 1/N. The proof then case-splits on whether i < j or i > j (via `Nat.lt_or_gt_of_ne`), setting q = |i-j| and p = ⌋iα⌋ - ⌋jα⌋. The key algebraic identity `fract_sub_eq` rewrites the fractional part difference as (i-j)α - (⌋iα⌋ - ⌋jα⌋), connecting the bin collision to the approximation quality. The `Nat.cast_sub` and `Int.cast_sub` lemmas handle the coercion gymnastics between ℕ, ℤ, and ℝ.
mathContext: **Dirichlet's Theorem**: $\forall \alpha \in \mathbb{R},\ \forall N \geq 1,\ \exists p \in \mathbb{Z},\ q \in \mathbb{N}$ with $1 \leq q \leq N$ and $|q\alpha - p| < 1/N$. Equivalently, $|\alpha - p/q| < 1/(qN) \leq 1/q^2$. The proof uses $N+1$ values $\{0\cdot\alpha\}, \{1\cdot\alpha\}, \ldots, \{N\cdot\alpha\}$ mapped to $N$ bins by $\lfloor N \cdot \{k\alpha\} \rfloor$. By pigeonhole, two collide, giving the approximation.

title: Nearest Integer Approximation Bound
content: A simple but foundational corollary: every real number has an integer within distance 1/2. The proof uses p = ⌊α + 1/2⌋, centering the floor function at the midpoint between consecutive integers. While elementary, this result is the N=1 case of Dirichlet's theorem (with the stronger bound 1/2 instead of 1/1), and it illustrates how floor/ceiling arguments yield approximation guarantees. In higher dimensions, this generalizes to Babai's nearest plane algorithm for lattice closest vector approximation.
mathContext: For any $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$, $\exists p \in \mathbb{Z}$ with $|\alpha - p| \leq 1/2$. Take $p = \lfloor \alpha + 1/2 \rfloor$. This is optimal: equality holds when $\alpha$ is a half-integer.

title: Lattice Point Existence in Intervals
content: `integer_in_interval` proves any interval [a, a+1) contains an integer (via the ceiling function). `lattice_point_exists` generalizes: for m > 0, the interval (a, a+m] contains a multiple of m. The proof divides by m, finds the appropriate integer via ⌊a/m⌋ + 1, and scales back. The `nlinarith` calls handle the resulting arithmetic involving floor division bounds. This connects to Minkowski's lattice point theorem and provides the geometric foundation for CRT solvability: existence of solutions to simultaneous congruences reduces to finding lattice points in shifted cosets.
mathContext: For $m > 0$ and $a \in \mathbb{R}$: $\exists k \in \mathbb{Z}$ with $a < km \leq a + m$. Proof: set $k = \lfloor a/m \rfloor + 1$. Then $a/m < k \leq a/m + 1$, so $a < km \leq a + m$.

title: Stern-Brocot Mediant and Farey Neighbors
content: `mediant_between` proves the mediant (a+c)/(b+d) lies strictly between a/b and c/d when a/b < c/d. The proof uses cross-multiplication: a/b < c/d implies ad < cb, then `nlinarith` derives the two mediant inequalities. `farey_neighbor_order` proves that Farey neighbors (fractions with determinant cb - ad = 1) are automatically ordered. The determinant condition cb - ad = 1 immediately implies ad < cb, giving a/b < c/d. The Stern-Brocot tree generates all positive rationals in lowest terms using the mediant operation, and Farey neighbors are adjacent fractions in Farey sequences F_n — they appear consecutively when ordered by denominator bound.
mathContext: For $a/b < c/d$ with $b, d > 0$: $a/b < (a+c)/(b+d) < c/d$. The mediant is the simplest fraction between two fractions. **Farey neighbors**: if $cb - ad = 1$, then $a/b$ and $c/d$ are adjacent in the Stern-Brocot tree and in the Farey sequence $F_{\max(b,d)}$.

title: Golden Ratio: The Worst-Case Approximation Target
content: Defines φ = (1+√5)/2 and proves its key algebraic properties: φ > 0, φ > 1, φ² = φ + 1, 1/φ = φ - 1, and φ² - φ - 1 = 0. The `golden_ratio_quadratic` proof uses `ring_nf` followed by `nlinarith` with `sq_sqrt` to establish φ² = φ + 1 from (√5)² = 5. The `golden_ratio_reciprocal` follows from `div_eq_iff` and the quadratic identity. Fibonacci examples (`native_decide`) verify fib(1)=1, fib(5)=5, fib(8)=21, fib(10)=55 — the denominators of φ's best rational approximations. The golden ratio is the hardest-to-approximate irrational because its continued fraction [1;1,1,...] has all partial quotients equal to 1, giving the slowest convergent convergence. Hurwitz (1891) proved |x - p/q| < 1/(√5 · q²) for infinitely many p/q, and √5 is optimal (achieved by φ).
mathContext: $\varphi = (1+\sqrt{5})/2$ satisfies $\varphi^2 = \varphi + 1$ (the minimal polynomial $x^2 - x - 1 = 0$). Its continued fraction $[1;1,1,\ldots]$ gives convergents $p_n/q_n = F_{n+1}/F_n$ (Fibonacci ratios). Hurwitz's theorem: $\forall$ irrational $\alpha$, $\exists^\infty p/q$ with $|\alpha - p/q| < 1/(\sqrt{5} q^2)$, and $\sqrt{5}$ is the best constant (attained by $\varphi$).

title: CRT Non-Coprime Lattice Examples
content: Concrete examples connecting CRT solvability to lattice coset membership. The solvable system x ≡ 3 (mod 6), x ≡ 1 (mod 4) has solution x = 9 (mod 12) because gcd(6,4) = 2 divides 3-1 = 2. The unsolvable system x ≡ 3 (mod 6), x ≡ 2 (mod 4) fails because gcd(6,4) = 2 does not divide 3-2 = 1. Bézout's identity 6·(-1) + 4·2 = 2 provides the coefficient witness. The Sunzi example (3rd century CE) x ≡ 2 (mod 3), x ≡ 3 (mod 5), x ≡ 2 (mod 7) → x = 23 (mod 105) demonstrates the classical CRT for coprime moduli. All examples use `native_decide` for computational verification.
mathContext: **CRT non-coprime solvability**: $x \equiv a_1 \pmod{m_1},\ x \equiv a_2 \pmod{m_2}$ is solvable $\iff \gcd(m_1, m_2) \mid (a_1 - a_2)$. When solvable, the solution is unique modulo $\text{lcm}(m_1, m_2)$. Geometrically: the solution set is the intersection of two cosets in $\mathbb{Z}$, which is nonempty iff the cosets are compatible modulo $\gcd$.
